key_terms.meaning: No device working in a cycle can take heat from one reservoir and convert it fully into work; some heat must always be rejected to a colder sink.
No device working in a cycle can move heat from a cold body to a hot body with zero work input.
A cyclic device that absorbs Q<sub>H</sub> from a hot reservoir at T<sub>H</sub>, rejects Q<sub>C</sub> to a cold reservoir at T<sub>C</sub>, and delivers W = Q<sub>H</sub> − Q<sub>C</sub>.
A cyclic device that takes Q<sub>C</sub> from a cold space and dumps Q<sub>H</sub> = Q<sub>C</sub> + W to the surroundings using work W.
A refrigerator whose useful output is the heat Q<sub>H</sub> delivered to the hot space; COP<sub>HP</sub> = Q<sub>H</sub>/W = COP<sub>R</sub> + 1.
Useful heat moved divided by work input: COP<sub>R</sub> = Q<sub>C</sub>/W for a refrigerator, COP<sub>HP</sub> = Q<sub>H</sub>/W for a heat pump.
A fully reversible cycle of two isothermal and two adiabatic steps between T<sub>H</sub> and T<sub>C</sub>; efficiency η = 1 − T<sub>C</sub>/T<sub>H</sub>.
No cycle between two fixed reservoirs beats a reversible one, and all reversible cycles between them have the same efficiency; η depends only on T<sub>H</sub> and T<sub>C</sub>.
A scale fixed only by reversible heat ratios, T<sub>C</sub>/T<sub>H</sub> = Q<sub>C</sub>/Q<sub>H</sub>, independent of the working fluid.
State function S with dS = δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T for a reversible path; for a real path ΔS > ∫δQ/T. Units J/K.
For any cycle, ∮δQ/T ≤ 0; the equality holds only when the cycle is fully reversible.
S<sub>gen</sub> is the entropy created by irreversibility inside a process; S<sub>gen</sub> ≥ 0, and S<sub>gen</sub> = 0 only for a reversible process.
A perfect crystal at 0 K has zero entropy; entropy changes vanish as T → 0, so absolute entropies can be tabulated.
Work destroyed by irreversibility, W<sub>lost</sub> = T₀ S<sub>gen</sub>, where T₀ is the surroundings temperature in K.
The practical steam power cycle: pump, boiler, turbine, condenser, with efficiency η = (W<sub>T</sub> − W<sub>P</sub>)/Q<sub>in</sub>.
Bleeding part of the steam from the turbine to preheat boiler feed water, raising the mean temperature of heat addition and hence η.
Temperature change on throttling at constant enthalpy; μ<sub>JT</sub> = (∂T/∂P)<sub>H</sub> is positive below the inversion temperature, so the gas cools.
Liquefaction cycle that cools the gas in a counter-current heat exchanger and expands part of it in an engine to make work, giving a higher liquid yield than simple throttling.
One specific microscopic arrangement of the molecules of a system; a macrostate is a set of microstates with the same measured properties.
Entropy still present at 0 K when a crystal is not perfect, for example because molecules freeze in random orientations.

takeaways: The second law is a statement about direction: work can turn completely into heat, but heat cannot turn completely into work in a cycle.
A heat engine, a refrigerator and a heat pump are the same energy balance read in three different directions.
The Carnot efficiency 1 − T<sub>C</sub>/T<sub>H</sub> is a ceiling set only by reservoir temperatures, not by the fluid or the machine.
Entropy is a state function; ΔS = ∫δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T over any convenient reversible path between the same two states.
The Clausius inequality ∮δQ/T ≤ 0 is the seed from which the whole entropy concept grows.
For a control volume, entropy carried in by flow and heat plus entropy generated equals entropy carried out plus accumulation.
Every real process destroys work equal to T₀ S<sub>gen</sub>, and that gap is what a second-law (exergy) analysis measures.
Real power plants and refrigerators are engineered by pushing their cycles closer to the reversible ideal — reheat, regeneration, and careful choice of boiler, condenser and evaporator pressures.
Entropy counts microstates: S = k<sub>B</sub> ln Ω, which is zero for a perfect crystal at 0 K and gives R ln 2 when a mole of gas doubles its volume.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the two statements with the proof of their equivalence, entropy-change calculations, the control-volume entropy balance, the third law with its microscopic meaning, and a steam power plant worked from steam tables. Long answers are marked for a clear sketch, each formula with its symbols, and every number carried with units.

bank.q: State the Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements of the second law and prove that they are equivalent.
outline: Both statements exactly, with the word cyclic
A Kelvin–Planck violator driving a refrigerator breaks Clausius
A Clausius violator paired with an engine breaks Kelvin–Planck
Conclusion: the two statements stand or fall together
answer: Kelvin–Planck statement. No device working in a cycle can take heat from a single reservoir and convert all of it into work. Some heat must be rejected to a colder reservoir, so for every heat engine W < QH and η < 1.
Clausius statement. No device working in a cycle can transfer heat from a colder body to a hotter body without work input. A refrigerator moves heat upward only because a compressor supplies work.

Both statements speak of a cyclic device. A single process can do what they forbid: a gas expanding isothermally turns all the heat it takes into work, but it ends in a different state, so it is not a cycle.
To prove equivalence, show that breaking either statement lets you build a device that breaks the other. Then "not KP ⇒ not Clausius" and "not Clausius ⇒ not KP", so KP ⇔ Clausius.

answer.text: Part 1: a Kelvin–Planck violator makes a Clausius violator. Let engine E take QH from the hot reservoir and deliver W = QH, rejecting nothing. Use W to drive an ordinary refrigerator R between the same reservoirs; R takes QC from the cold reservoir and rejects QC + W to the hot reservoir. Treat E + R as one device:

answer: The pair moves Q<sub>C</sub> from cold to hot with zero net work. That is exactly what the Clausius statement forbids. With numbers: if E takes 100 kJ and gives 100 kJ, and R has COP<sub>R</sub> = 3, then R lifts 300 kJ and rejects 400 kJ; the hot reservoir gains 300 kJ, the cold one loses 300 kJ, and no work is used.

answer.text: Part 2: a Clausius violator makes a Kelvin–Planck violator. Let device C move QC from the cold to the hot reservoir with no work. Run an ordinary engine E between the same reservoirs, adjusted so that it rejects exactly QC; it takes QH and gives W = QH − QC.

answer: The cold reservoir is unchanged, so the pair takes heat Q<sub>H</sub> − Q<sub>C</sub> from the hot reservoir alone and turns all of it into work in a cycle. That breaks the Kelvin–Planck statement.

Sketch for each part: two reservoirs as horizontal boxes, the two devices as circles between them, arrows for every heat and work flow with its label, and a dashed outline round the pair to show the combined device.

Conclusion: each statement implies the other, so they are two forms of one law. Kelvin–Planck is the form used for engines (η < 1), Clausius the form used for refrigerators (COP is finite). Check of the numbers in Part 1: energy is conserved, since +300 − 300 + 0 = 0, so only the second law is broken.

bank.q: Starting from the Carnot cycle, show that ∮δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T = 0 for any reversible cycle and hence that entropy is a state function. Explain how ΔS is calculated for an irreversible process.
outline: Q<sub>H</sub>/T<sub>H</sub> = Q<sub>C</sub>/T<sub>C</sub> for a Carnot cycle
Any reversible cycle as a set of thin Carnot cycles
Zero cyclic integral means path independence
Irreversible process: use a reversible path between the same end states
answer: For a reversible (Carnot) engine between T<sub>H</sub> and T<sub>C</sub>, the thermodynamic temperature scale gives Q<sub>H</sub>/Q<sub>C</sub> = T<sub>H</sub>/T<sub>C</sub>, so Q<sub>H</sub>/T<sub>H</sub> = Q<sub>C</sub>/T<sub>C</sub>.

Count heat into the system as positive. Over one Carnot cycle the heat crosses only at T<sub>H</sub> (+Q<sub>H</sub>) and T<sub>C</sub> (−Q<sub>C</sub>), so Σ Q/T = Q<sub>H</sub>/T<sub>H</sub> − Q<sub>C</sub>/T<sub>C</sub> = 0.

Any reversible cycle drawn on P–V axes can be covered by a large number of thin Carnot cycles made of isotherms and adiabats. Neighbouring adiabats are traversed in opposite directions, so their contributions cancel, and the outer zig-zag path approaches the real cycle as the strips get thinner.
Each strip gives δQ<sub>H</sub>/T<sub>H</sub> − δQ<sub>C</sub>/T<sub>C</sub> = 0, so adding them all: ∮δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T = 0 for every reversible cycle.

answer.text: Path independence: take two states 1 and 2 and two reversible paths A and B between them. Going 1→2 along A and back 2→1 along B makes a reversible cycle:
answer.pre:
∫(1→2, A) δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T + ∫(2→1, B) δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T = 0
∫(1→2, A) δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T = ∫(1→2, B) δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T

answer: The integral depends only on the end states, so it is the change of a property. Define dS = δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T and ΔS = ∫₁² δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T. Q and W are path functions; S, like U, is a state function.

Irreversible process: the actual δQ/T does not give ΔS. Because S is a state function, pick any reversible path between the same end states and integrate along it. The Clausius inequality then says ΔS ≥ ∫δQ/T for the real path.

Example: 1 mol of ideal gas at 300 K expands freely from 10 L to 20 L (Q = 0, W = 0, T unchanged). The reversible isotherm between the same states gives ΔS = R ln(V₂/V₁) = 8.314 × 0.6931 = 5.76 J/K. The real ∫δQ/T is 0, which is less than 5.76 J/K, as the inequality requires; S<sub>gen</sub> = 5.76 J/K.

Two paths, one ΔS. Check path independence with the same end states (1 mol of a diatomic ideal gas, 300 K, 10 L → 20 L, CV = 5R/2 = 20.785 J/K, γ = 1.4). Path A, reversible isotherm: ΔS = 5.76 J/K as above. Path B: a reversible adiabatic expansion from 10 L to 20 L (ΔS = 0) cools the gas to T′ = 300 × (10/20)0.4 = 227.36 K; then reversible heating at constant volume back to 300 K gives ΔS = CV ln(300/227.36) = 20.785 × 0.27726 = 5.76 J/K.

Both paths give 5.76 J/K even though their heat flows differ (1728.8 J on path A; C<sub>V</sub> × 72.64 = 1509.9 J on path B). Q depends on the path; Q<sub>rev</sub>/T summed along any reversible path does not, which is what a state function means.
Check with the reversible isotherm itself: Q<sub>rev</sub> = RT ln 2 = 8.314 × 300 × 0.6931 = 1728.8 J, and Q<sub>rev</sub>/T = 1728.8/300 = 5.76 J/K, the same ΔS.

bank.q: State the third law of thermodynamics and explain, using S = k<sub>B</sub> ln Ω, why a perfect crystal has zero entropy at 0 K while carbon monoxide and ice keep a residual entropy. Show how absolute entropies are built from heat-capacity data.
outline: Ω = 1 gives S = 0; frozen-in orientations give Ω > 1
Residual entropy of CO and ice with numbers
S(T) from the Debye part, ∫C<sub>p</sub>/T dT and transition terms
answer: Third law. The entropy of a perfect, ordered crystal is zero at 0 K. A consequence is that 0 K cannot be reached in a finite number of steps.

Microscopic meaning. Boltzmann: S = kB ln Ω, where Ω is the number of microstates that give the same macrostate and kB = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K. In a perfect crystal at 0 K every molecule sits in its lowest-energy position in one arrangement, so Ω = 1 and S = kB ln 1 = 0.

Carbon monoxide. CO is nearly symmetric, so each molecule can sit as CO or OC with almost the same energy, and cooling freezes a random mixture. If each of the NA molecules in a mole had 2 equally likely orientations, Ω = 2NA and S = kB NA ln 2 = R ln 2 = 8.314 × 0.6931 = 5.76 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. The measured value is about 4.6 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, a little smaller because the freezing is not perfectly random.

Ice. The hydrogen atoms can be arranged in many ways that all obey the hydrogen-bond rules. Pauling counted about (3/2)NA arrangements per mole, giving S(0) = R ln 1.5 = 8.314 × 0.4055 = 3.37 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, close to the measured value. Glasses also keep frozen disorder. None of this breaks the third law: these solids are not perfect crystals.

answer.text: Absolute entropy from data. With S(0) = 0, heat reversibly at constant pressure and add every piece:
answer.pre:
S(T) = aT₁³/3 + ∫(T₁→T<sub>m</sub>) C<sub>p,s</sub>/T dT + ΔH<sub>fus</sub>/T<sub>m</sub> + ∫(T<sub>m</sub>→T) C<sub>p,l</sub>/T dT
(below T₁ ≈ 10 K, C<sub>p</sub> = aT³, so that piece is C<sub>p</sub>(T₁)/3)

answer.text: Worked numbers (the third-law chapter data): C<sub>p</sub>(10 K) = 0.80, solid integral 60.0, ΔH<sub>fus</sub> = 8.00 kJ/mol at 200 K, liquid C<sub>p</sub> = 120 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

answer: Why the third law is needed: without a fixed zero, calorimetry gives only differences. With S(0) = 0, tables can list absolute entropies S° that are used directly in reaction-equilibrium calculations. Check: each piece is positive, and the melting step is large because ΔH/T for a phase change is concentrated at one temperature.

bank.q: Explain the microscopic meaning of entropy using S = k<sub>B</sub> ln Ω for N labelled gas molecules in a box with two equal halves. Show that the result for one mole doubling its volume agrees with the classical ΔS = R ln(V₂/V₁).
outline: Even split is the most probable macrostate
answer: A microstate says where every labelled molecule is (here: left or right half). A macrostate is what we measure, here n, the number of molecules in the left half.

Each molecule has 2 choices, so the box has 2<sup>N</sup> microstates in all. The number giving n molecules on the left is Ω(n) = N!/[n!(N − n)!]. At fixed U, V and N every microstate is equally likely, so the macrostate with the largest Ω is the one we observe.

answer.text: N = 4: Ω = 1, 4, 6, 4, 1 for n = 0 to 4 (total 16). N = 10: the all-left macrostate has Ω = 1, the even split has Ω = 252, out of 1024.

answer: As N grows, the even split takes an ever larger share and the chance that all molecules gather in one half, (1/2)<sup>N</sup>, becomes vanishingly small. This is why a gas spreads to fill its container and never un-mixes: the process goes towards larger Ω, that is larger S.
One mole doubling its volume. Each of the NA molecules now has twice as many places, so Ω₂/Ω₁ = 2NA. ΔS = kB ln(Ω₂/Ω₁) = kB NA ln 2 = R ln 2.

Classical result for an isothermal ideal gas: ΔS = R ln(V₂/V₁) = R ln 2 = 8.314 × 0.6931 = 5.76 J/K. The two routes agree, because R = N<sub>A</sub> k<sub>B</sub> = 6.022 × 10²³ × 1.381 × 10⁻²³ = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Probability of un-mixing. With N = 10 the chance of finding all molecules on the left is 1/1024 = 0.00098; with N = 100 it is (1/2)100 = 7.9 × 10⁻³¹. For a mole it is never seen.

For large N, Stirling's formula ln N! ≈ N ln N − N gives ln Ω(N/2) ≈ N ln 2, the same as ln 2<sup>N</sup> for the whole box. For N = 100 the exact values are ln Ω(50) = 66.78 and 100 ln 2 = 69.31, already within 4 %. So the even-split macrostate carries almost all the entropy of the gas.
Note: entropy is not "disorder" in a visual sense; it is the logarithm of the number of accessible microstates. Because of the logarithm, doubling Ω adds only k<sub>B</sub> ln 2 to S.

bank.q: A Carnot engine works between 800 K and 300 K and receives 500 kJ from the hot reservoir per cycle. Find the efficiency, the work and the heat rejected. Then find the COP of a Carnot refrigerator and of a Carnot heat pump working between the same two temperatures, and comment.
outline: W and Q<sub>C</sub> with an energy check
answer: Data: T<sub>H</sub> = 800 K, T<sub>C</sub> = 300 K, Q<sub>H</sub> = 500 kJ. Temperatures are already in kelvin.
Carnot efficiency: η = 1 − T<sub>C</sub>/T<sub>H</sub> = 1 − 300/800 = 1 − 0.375 = 0.625, that is 62.5 %.
Work: W = η Q<sub>H</sub> = 0.625 × 500 = 312.5 kJ.
Heat rejected: Q<sub>C</sub> = Q<sub>H</sub> − W = 500 − 312.5 = 187.5 kJ. Ratio check: Q<sub>C</sub>/Q<sub>H</sub> = 187.5/500 = 0.375 = T<sub>C</sub>/T<sub>H</sub>.
Entropy check: the hot reservoir loses 500/800 = 0.625 kJ/K and the cold one gains 187.5/300 = 0.625 kJ/K, so the total entropy change is zero, as it must be for a reversible cycle.
Carnot refrigerator between the same temperatures: COP<sub>R</sub> = T<sub>C</sub>/(T<sub>H</sub> − T<sub>C</sub>) = 300/(800 − 300) = 300/500 = 0.60.
Carnot heat pump: COP<sub>HP</sub> = T<sub>H</sub>/(T<sub>H</sub> − T<sub>C</sub>) = 800/500 = 1.60 = COP<sub>R</sub> + 1.

Comment: COP<sub>R</sub> is below 1 here because the lift from 300 K to 800 K is very large; every kJ moved costs 1/0.6 = 1.67 kJ of work. COP is not an efficiency and can be above or below 1. With the reversed engine, 312.5 kJ of work would lift 187.5 kJ from 300 K and deliver 500 kJ at 800 K, exactly undoing the engine.

Which change helps more? Lowering TC by 10 K gives η = 1 − 290/800 = 0.6375; raising TH by 10 K gives η = 1 − 300/810 = 0.6296. Lowering the cold temperature helps more, because η depends on the ratio TC/TH.

Why the result holds for any working fluid: the Carnot theorem says every reversible engine between the same two reservoirs has the same efficiency, so 62.5 % is the limit whether the engine uses steam, air or an ideal gas. Only the reservoir temperatures, in kelvin, enter the answer.

A real engine for comparison. If a real engine gave 250 kJ from the same 500 kJ, η = 0.50 and the second-law efficiency is 0.50/0.625 = 0.80. It rejects 250 kJ, so Sgen = 250/300 − 500/800 = 0.8333 − 0.6250 = 0.2083 kJ/K, and the lost work TC Sgen = 300 × 0.2083 = 62.5 kJ equals 312.5 − 250, as it should.
Sketch: two reservoirs at 800 K and 300 K with the engine between them (500 in, 312.5 out as work, 187.5 rejected), and the same diagram with all arrows reversed for the refrigerator.

bank.q: 2 kg of water is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 350 K by a reservoir at 360 K. Later the same 2 kg of water, at 273 K, is frozen in a freezer whose surroundings are at 263 K (latent heat 334 kJ/kg). Take c<sub>p</sub> = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K). For each process find ΔS of the water, ΔS of the reservoir and S<sub>gen</sub>.
outline: Reversible substitute path for the water
answer: The water is the system. Its ΔS uses a reversible path between the same end states; each reservoir stays at one temperature, so its ΔS is Q/T<sub>reservoir</sub> with the sign of the heat it receives.
Heat supplied: Q = m cp (T₂ − T₁) = 2 × 4.18 × 50 = 418 kJ, taken from the 360 K reservoir.
Entropy generated: Sgen = 1.2887 − 1.1611 = 0.1276 kJ/K > 0. The heating is irreversible because heat crosses from 360 K to water that is between 300 and 350 K.
Freezing, water: at 273 K the latent heat leaves the water: ΔS = −m L/T = −2 × 334/273 = −668/273 = −2.4469 kJ/K. A fall in the system entropy is allowed; only the total must rise.
Freezer space: the cold space at 263 K receives the 668 kJ, so ΔS = +668/263 = +2.5399 kJ/K.
Entropy generated: Sgen = −2.4469 + 2.5399 = 0.0930 kJ/K > 0.

A closer reservoir. If the water were heated by a reservoir at 350 K instead, ΔSreservoir = −418/350 = −1.1943 kJ/K and Sgen = 1.2887 − 1.1943 = 0.0944 kJ/K. The smaller the temperature gap across which heat flows, the smaller Sgen.

The freezer itself. The 668 kJ that entered the 263 K space must be pumped out to a kitchen, say at 298 K. A Carnot refrigerator needs at least W = 668 × (298 − 263)/263 = 88.9 kJ for that (COP = 263/35 = 7.51). A real freezer with a lower COP needs more, and every extra kJ of work raises the entropy of the kitchen.

Sketch for each process: the water as a box, the reservoir or freezer space as a larger box at its fixed temperature, and one heat arrow (418 kJ into the water, 668 kJ out of it) labelled with Q and the temperature it crosses at.

Check: both S<sub>gen</sub> are positive, so both processes are possible; S<sub>gen</sub> would fall to zero only if the reservoir temperature followed the water temperature at every instant. The units are kJ/K throughout because m c<sub>p</sub> is in kJ/K.

bank.q: Steam enters an insulated turbine at 4 MPa and 500 °C and leaves at 10 kPa with a quality of 0.90. Take the surroundings at 298 K. Find the work, the entropy generated per kg, the lost work, the ideal work and the isentropic efficiency.
outline: w = h₁ − h₂ for the adiabatic turbine
s<sub>gen</sub> = s₂ − s₁, lost work = T₀ s<sub>gen</sub>
answer: Energy balance, steady, adiabatic, kinetic energy neglected: w = h₁ − h₂ = 3445.8 − 2344.7 = 1101.1 kJ/kg.
Entropy balance per kg, adiabatic: s<sub>gen</sub> = s₂ − s₁ = 7.3989 − 7.0919 = 0.3070 kJ/(kg·K). It is positive, so the turbine is irreversible but possible.
Lost work (Gouy–Stodola): w<sub>lost</sub> = T₀ s<sub>gen</sub> = 298 × 0.3070 = 91.5 kJ/kg.

Ideal work between the same two states (work input positive): W<sub>ideal</sub> = Δh − T₀Δs = (2344.7 − 3445.8) − 298 × 0.3070 = −1101.1 − 91.5 = −1192.6 kJ/kg, so the best possible output is 1192.6 kJ/kg; the second-law efficiency is 1101.1/1192.6 = 0.923.

Note the two efficiencies differ: η<sub>t</sub> compares with an isentropic turbine ending at the same pressure; the second-law efficiency compares with a reversible process ending in the same actual state, with heat exchanged with the surroundings at T₀.

head: Quantity
Value
rows: ideal work (to the actual exit state)

answer: For a plant flow of 10 kg/s: power 10 × 1101.1 = 11 011 kW = 11.0 MW, and lost work 10 × 91.5 = 915 kW. The second-law efficiency is a little higher than η<sub>t</sub> because the actual exit steam (s₂ > s<sub>2s</sub>) still holds some work potential that a reversible device could recover by exchanging heat with the surroundings.

Check: w<sub>ideal</sub> − w = 1192.6 − 1101.1 = 91.5 kJ/kg = T₀ s<sub>gen</sub>. Sketch: T–s diagram with the dome, state 1 superheated, 2s straight below it at 10 kPa, and 2 to the right of 2s on the same 10 kPa line.

bank.q: An ideal Rankine cycle has steam at 10 MPa and 500 °C at the turbine inlet and a condenser at 10 kPa. Find the pump work, turbine work, heat added, efficiency and exhaust quality. Then add reheat at 1 MPa to 500 °C and find the new efficiency and exhaust quality. Sketch both cycles on T–s axes.
outline: States from steam tables; w<sub>p</sub> = v<sub>f</sub> Δp
Reheat: two turbine stages, two heat additions

answer.text: Data (IAPWS-IF97). At 10 kPa: h<sub>f</sub> = 191.8 kJ/kg, v<sub>f</sub> = 0.001010 m³/kg, s<sub>f</sub> = 0.6492, s<sub>fg</sub> = 7.4997 kJ/(kg·K), h<sub>fg</sub> = 2392.1 kJ/kg, T<sub>sat</sub> = 45.8 °C.

answer: η = 1275.3/3173.2 = 0.402, that is 40.2 %. Exhaust quality 0.79 is too wet for the last blades (designers want about 0.88 or more).
With reheat: high-pressure turbine 3375.1 − 2783.6 = 591.5 kJ/kg (the steam just reaches 1 MPa as slightly superheated vapour at 182.3 °C). Reheat adds 3479.0 − 2783.6 = 695.4 kJ/kg.

Reheat raised the efficiency by about one percentage point and, more importantly, dried the exhaust from 0.79 to 0.95; it also raised the work per kg by 25 %, so less steam is needed for the same power.

Heat rejected, and an energy check. Simple cycle: q<sub>out</sub> = h₄ − h₁ = 2089.6 − 191.8 = 1897.8 kJ/kg, and q<sub>in</sub> − q<sub>out</sub> = 3173.2 − 1897.8 = 1275.4 kJ/kg ≈ w<sub>net</sub> (rounding). Reheat cycle: q<sub>out</sub> = 2461.1 − 191.8 = 2269.3 kJ/kg, and 3868.5 − 2269.3 = 1599.2 kJ/kg = w<sub>net</sub>.
Steam flow for a 100 MW plant: 100 000/1275.3 = 78.4 kg/s without reheat and 100 000/1599.2 = 62.5 kg/s with reheat.

Sketch: T–s dome; simple cycle 1-2-3-4 with a vertical turbine line from 500 °C to 45.8 °C ending deep in the dome; reheat cycle with a short vertical drop to the 1 MPa line, a heating curve back to 500 °C, and a second vertical drop ending near the saturated-vapour line.

bank.q: An ideal vapour-compression refrigerator uses R-134a with the evaporator at −10 °C and the condenser at 40 °C. Find the refrigerating effect, compressor work, condenser duty and COP per kg, compare with the Carnot COP, and find the COP if the compressor is 80 % efficient.
outline: Carnot COP and the effect of compressor efficiency

answer.text: R-134a values (tables with h = 200 kJ/kg for saturated liquid at 0 °C; any other reference shifts every h equally and gives the same COP):

answer: Refrigerating effect: q<sub>L</sub> = h₁ − h₄ = 392.7 − 256.4 = 136.3 kJ/kg.
Compressor work (isentropic): w = h₂ − h₁ = 426.5 − 392.7 = 33.8 kJ/kg.
Condenser duty: q<sub>H</sub> = h₂ − h₃ = 426.5 − 256.4 = 170.1 kJ/kg = q<sub>L</sub> + w.

Carnot COP between 263.15 K and 313.15 K: 263.15/50 = 5.26. The ideal vapour cycle reaches 4.03/5.26 = 0.77 of it. The loss comes from the throttle (an irreversible expansion that wastes the work a turbine could recover) and from rejecting heat from superheated vapour at up to 46.3 °C instead of 40 °C.
Compressor efficiency 0.80: actual work = 33.8/0.80 = 42.3 kJ/kg, so COP = 136.3/42.3 = 3.22. The condenser must now reject 136.3 + 42.3 = 178.6 kJ/kg.

Why real COP is lower still: pressure drops in the pipes, superheat in the suction line, heat exchangers that need a temperature difference, so the refrigerant evaporates below the space temperature and condenses above the ambient.

Sizing for a 10 kW cooling load: refrigerant flow ṁ = 10/136.3 = 0.0734 kg/s; compressor power 0.0734 × 33.8 = 2.48 kW ideal and 0.0734 × 42.3 = 3.10 kW real. The load is 10/3.517 = 2.84 tonnes of refrigeration.
Check: for each case condenser duty = refrigerating effect + work (136.3 + 33.8 = 170.1 and 136.3 + 42.3 = 178.6 kJ/kg), and both COPs are below the Carnot value 5.26.
Sketch: P–h diagram with the dome, horizontal lines at 0.20 and 1.02 MPa, the compressor line 1→2 sloping up and right, condenser 2→3 to the liquid line, and a vertical throttle 3→4.

bank.q: Two water streams, 1 kg/s at 350 K and 1 kg/s at 290 K, mix adiabatically at steady state. Take c<sub>p</sub> = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K) and T₀ = 290 K. Find the exit temperature, the entropy generated and the lost work. Then find the work a reversible engine could produce if it brought the two streams to a common temperature instead, and explain the difference.
outline: S<sub>gen</sub> from the two stream entropy changes
Reversible engine: common temperature √(T₁T₂) and its work
answer: Energy balance: equal flows and equal c<sub>p</sub>, so T<sub>out</sub> = (350 + 290)/2 = 320 K.
Steady, adiabatic mixer: S<sub>gen</sub> = Σṁ_out s<sub>out</sub> − Σṁ_in s<sub>in</sub> = ṁc<sub>p</sub> ln(T<sub>out</sub>/T₁) + ṁc<sub>p</sub> ln(T<sub>out</sub>/T₂).
S<sub>gen</sub> = −0.3746 + 0.4115 = 0.0369 kW/K > 0: mixing is irreversible.
Lost work: W<sub>lost</sub> = T₀S<sub>gen</sub> = 290 × 0.0369 = 10.7 kW.

Reversible alternative: let the hot stream feed a reversible engine whose cold side is the cold stream. With no entropy generated, ln(T<sub>f</sub>/350) + ln(T<sub>f</sub>/290) = 0, so T<sub>f</sub> = √(350 × 290) = 318.6 K.
Work from the energy balance: W = ṁc<sub>p</sub>(350 − T<sub>f</sub>) − ṁc<sub>p</sub>(T<sub>f</sub> − 290) = 4.18 × (640 − 2 × 318.6) = 4.18 × 2.82 = 11.8 kW.

Why 11.8 kW and not 10.7 kW: the two answers use different end states. The reversible engine ends with both streams at 318.6 K, not 320 K, because it has turned part of the energy into work. The lost work 10.7 kW is measured against a dead state at T₀ = 290 K for the mixer's own end state. Both say the same thing: mixing at a 60 K difference throws away about 11 kW of work potential.

Exergy check. Flow exergy of liquid water relative to T₀ = 290 K: ṁcp[(T − T₀) − T₀ ln(T/T₀)]. Hot inlet: 4.18 × [60 − 290 × ln(350/290)] = 4.18 × (60 − 54.535) = 22.84 kW. Cold inlet at T₀: 0. Exit, 2 kg/s at 320 K: 8.36 × [30 − 290 × ln(320/290)] = 8.36 × (30 − 28.548) = 12.14 kW.
Exergy destroyed = 22.84 + 0 − 12.14 = 10.70 kW, the same as T₀S<sub>gen</sub>. So almost half of the hot stream's work potential is lost in the mixer.

Evaluation: in plant design this is why hot and cold streams are matched in heat exchangers with small temperature differences rather than mixed, and why waste heat at 350 K still has some value. Check: S<sub>gen</sub> small but positive; W<sub>lost</sub>/(ṁc<sub>p</sub>ΔT of the hot stream, 125.4 kW) is under 10 %, sensible for a 60 K gap near ambient.

bank.q: A salesman claims a cyclic device takes 100 kW of heat from a reservoir at 500 K, rejects heat to a reservoir at 300 K and delivers 60 kW of work. Test the claim with the first law, the Carnot limit and the Clausius inequality, and find the largest work the device could give.
answer: First law for a cycle: Q<sub>C</sub> = Q<sub>H</sub> − W = 100 − 60 = 40 kW. Energy balances, so the first law alone cannot reject the claim.
Claimed efficiency: η = W/Q<sub>H</sub> = 60/100 = 0.60.
Carnot limit between the same reservoirs: η<sub>max</sub> = 1 − 300/500 = 0.40. The claim (0.60) is above the limit, so it breaks the Carnot theorem and therefore the second law.
Clausius inequality: ∮δQ/T = Q<sub>H</sub>/T<sub>H</sub> − Q<sub>C</sub>/T<sub>C</sub> = 100/500 − 40/300 = 0.2000 − 0.1333 = +0.0667 kW/K. A positive value is impossible (it must be ≤ 0).

Same result as reservoir entropy: the hot reservoir changes by −100/500 = −0.2000 kW/K and the cold one by +40/300 = +0.1333 kW/K; total −0.0667 kW/K, a decrease of the entropy of an isolated system, which is impossible.
Largest possible work: a reversible device gives W<sub>max</sub> = 0.40 × 100 = 40 kW and rejects 60 kW; then ∮δQ/T = 100/500 − 60/300 = 0. Any real device gives less than 40 kW.
What would make 60 kW possible: a hotter source or a colder sink. With T<sub>C</sub> = 300 K, η = 0.60 needs T<sub>H</sub> ≥ 300/0.40 = 750 K.

answer.text: Rating three possible claims for the same 100 kW at 500 K:

answer: The test that needs no Carnot formula is the entropy of the two reservoirs: any proposed device can be judged from its three numbers Q<sub>H</sub>, Q<sub>C</sub> and W and the two temperatures. That is why the Clausius inequality is the general form of the second law.
For the 30 kW device: second-law efficiency 30/40 = 0.75, and lost work T<sub>C</sub> S<sub>gen</sub> = 300 × 0.0333 = 10 kW = 40 − 30. The entropy balance and the work balance tell the same story.

Sketch: hot reservoir at 500 K above, cold reservoir at 300 K below, the device as a circle between them with 100 kW in, the claimed 60 kW out as work and 40 kW rejected; mark the reversible case (40 kW work, 60 kW rejected) beside it for comparison.
Conclusion: reject the claim. Check of the three tests: all agree because the Carnot limit and the Clausius inequality are the same second law written two ways.

bank.q: Compare the Carnot and Rankine cycles for a steam power plant. Using the plant with steam at 4 MPa and 400 °C and a condenser at 10 kPa (η = 35.3 %), explain with the mean temperature of heat addition why the Rankine efficiency is lower, and evaluate how superheat, reheat, regeneration and condenser pressure each change it.
outline: Why a Carnot steam cycle is impractical
answer: A Carnot cycle needs all heat added at one top temperature and all heat rejected at one bottom temperature, with isentropic compression and expansion. With steam inside the dome that means compressing a wet mixture back to saturated liquid, which needs a large two-phase compressor, and a turbine running wet. Superheating at constant temperature is not practical either.

The Rankine cycle condenses fully and pumps liquid only (4.0 kJ/kg in the example, about 0.4 % of the turbine work), and adds heat at constant pressure. Heat is therefore added over a range of temperatures, from 45.9 °C feedwater up to 400 °C steam.

Mean temperature of heat addition: T<sub>m</sub> = q<sub>in</sub>/(s₃ − s₂) = 3018.6/(6.7712 − 0.6492) = 3018.6/6.1220 = 493.1 K. Heat is rejected at T<sub>low</sub> = 318.96 K (45.8 °C). Then η = 1 − T<sub>low</sub>/T<sub>m</sub> = 1 − 318.96/493.1 = 0.353, exactly the cycle efficiency.

So the Rankine cycle loses mainly because much of its heat goes in at low temperature (warming the feedwater from 46 °C to 250 °C). Every improvement either raises T<sub>m</sub> or lowers T<sub>low</sub>.
Superheat: raises the top temperature and so T<sub>m</sub>, and dries the exhaust. Limited by metal strength (about 540–600 °C in conventional plants).

Reheat: adds a second slice of heat at high temperature. For 10 MPa, 500 °C with reheat at 1 MPa to 500 °C, η rises from 40.2 % to 41.3 % and the exhaust quality from 0.79 to 0.95; the drier exhaust is the main reason to reheat.

Regeneration: bleed steam heats the feedwater, so the boiler no longer adds the low-temperature heat. T<sub>m</sub> rises, q<sub>in</sub> falls, and η rises by several percentage points in large plants; the cost is less work per kg of steam and the heaters.
Condenser pressure: lowering p<sub>c</sub> lowers T<sub>low</sub>. It is limited by the cooling-water temperature (near 30 °C in India), air leakage and the size of the last-stage blades.

Evaluation: superheat, reheat and regeneration all move the Rankine cycle toward the Carnot cycle between the same extremes while keeping its practical advantages (liquid pumping, dry turbine). Check: the T<sub>m</sub> method reproduces the computed 35.3 %, so the explanation is quantitative, not only qualitative.

glossary.def: A body large enough that taking or giving heat does not change its temperature.
Work output divided by heat input of a heat engine, η = W/Q<sub>H</sub>.
An ideal process whose direction can be reversed by an infinitesimal change, leaving no trace on the surroundings.
Any effect such as friction, unrestrained expansion or finite-temperature heat transfer that makes a process non-reversible and creates entropy.
A process of constant entropy, the ideal limit for an adiabatic reversible turbine or compressor.
Flow through a restriction with no work and negligible heat transfer, so enthalpy stays constant and pressure falls.
Liquefaction cycle that cools the gas in a counter-current exchanger and then expands it through a throttle valve.
μ<sub>JT</sub> = (∂T/∂P)<sub>H</sub>; positive means the gas cools on throttling.
Temperature at which μ<sub>JT</sub> changes sign; above it a gas warms on throttling.
Entropy measured from the third-law zero at 0 K, as listed in steam and property tables.
The measured, macroscopic description of a system (for example U, V and N) that many microstates can produce.
k<sub>B</sub> = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K, the entropy per unit of ln Ω.
The work a process would need or deliver if it were fully reversible, W<sub>ideal</sub> = W<sub>actual</sub> − W<sub>lost</sub>.
Ratio of actual performance to the best reversible performance under the same conditions.
A fixed region in space with mass and energy crossing its boundary; used for turbines, compressors and heat exchangers.
Condition where properties inside the control volume do not change with time, so accumulation terms vanish.
Heat exchanger in a power plant that adds Q<sub>in</sub> to pressurised water to make steam.
Heat exchanger that rejects Q<sub>out</sub> and condenses turbine exhaust back to liquid.
Heating steam above its saturation temperature at the same pressure.
The cold-side heat exchanger of a refrigerator where the refrigerant boils and absorbs Q<sub>C</sub>.
∮δQ/T ≤ 0 for any thermodynamic cycle.
An isentropic process, drawn as a vertical line on T–s coordinates.
Accounting statement: entropy in by flow and heat, plus generated entropy, equals entropy out plus accumulation.
